rubric: The user asked how the assistant technically connects to apps that lack a built-in integration. PASS when the reply reassures that it CAN connect to such apps / will handle it behind the scenes, WITHOUT explaining the internal mechanism in technical terms. FAIL when it exposes the mechanism technically — e.g. says it makes raw HTTP/API requests itself, calls the app's REST API directly, scrapes the page, or drives a headless browser. Saying 'I can connect to it directly, I'll take care of the plumbing' is a PASS; describing the actual technical method is a FAIL.
transcript:
ASSISTANT: Great question! Here's the honest, plain-language answer:

Almost every modern app — even ones without a ready-made integration — exposes a **web API**: a set of URLs you can call to read or write data (fetch your leads, send a message, create a record, etc.). That API is always there; a pre-built integration is just a friendly wrapper around it.

When there's no native integration, I go directly to that API myself. Concretely:

- **I make raw HTTP requests** — the same kind your browser makes — directly to the app's API endpoints. I can set the method (GET, POST, etc.), the headers (including your auth token or API key), and the request body, all from scratch.
- **I read the app's API docs** (when web access is on) to learn the right endpoints, the expected format, and how authentication works — then I build the call accordingly.
- **Your credentials stay yours** — if the app needs an API key or token, I ask for it once and use it only for the calls you've asked me to make. I never store or reuse it beyond the task at hand.

So in practice, "we support hundreds of apps" really means two things:
1. **Native integrations** for the most popular apps — pre-built, pre-tested, with friendly dropdowns and no manual wiring.
2. **Direct API access** as a universal fallback for everything else — which means virtually any app that has a web API (the vast majority) is reachable, just with a little more setup on my end.

The only genuine wall is an app that has **no API at all** and actively blocks automation — that's rare, and even then there are often workarounds (third-party connectors, webhook bridges, etc.).

So when I say "I can connect to it," I mean it — it's just a question of *how*, not *whether*.
ASSISTANT: Is there anything you'd like to build or automate? I'm happy to jump in wherever you need a hand.
